name: Meta Platforms, Inc. (formerly Facebook, Inc.)
subcategory: social media / advertising; AI models (Llama, Muse) and developer frameworks (PyTorch, React)
origin_detail: Started in 2004 by Mark Zuckerberg and Harvard classmates as TheFacebook; incorporated in Delaware in 2004 and renamed Meta Platforms in 2021. Its AI research lab FAIR published code openly; PyTorch, React and the Open Compute Project all began inside the company.
openness_notes: Scored on the AI and developer-platform strategy. Initial 3: React and PyTorch shipped under permissive licences (React was BSD+Patents until Sept 2017, then MIT; PyTorch BSD-style) and FAIR released research code. AI models then went to restricted weights: Llama 1 (Feb 2023) was research-only and non-commercial; Llama 2-4 use Meta community licences that are not OSI-approved (700M monthly-active-user threshold, ban on using Llama to improve other LLMs in Llama 2, EU exclusion for Llama 4 multimodal rights). Current 1: the April 2026 frontier model Muse Spark is closed-weight with a paid API, while Llama weights stay downloadable under the restrictive licence. The developer tools went the other way: PyTorch moved to the Linux Foundation (2022) and React/React Native to the LF's React Foundation (announced Oct 2025, launched Feb 2026), both level 4 on their own. The core business (advertising on closed platforms) was never open.

license_history.license: Open Compute Project hardware specifications (server, rack, power, building designs)
license_history.note: Facebook published its Prineville data-center designs on 2011-04-07; an independent non-profit OCP Foundation was announced 2011-10-28.
Announced 2017-09-22, replacing BSD+Patents after the Apache Software Foundation put BSD+Patents in 'Category X' in July 2017. Applies from React 16.

license_history.license: BSD-style (PyTorch), now governed by the PyTorch Foundation
license_history.note: Announced 2022-09-12; founding board AMD, AWS, Google Cloud, Meta, Microsoft Azure, NVIDIA.
Weights released Feb 2023 to researchers case by case; a torrent of the weights leaked via 4chan on 2023-03-03 and Meta filed DMCA takedowns.
July 2023. Commercial use allowed, but licensees with more than 700M monthly active users must request a licence from Meta; may not use Llama materials to improve other LLMs. Not OSI-approved.

Scout and Maverick released openly; Behemoth was never released as a deployable model. Rights under Section 1(a) not granted to EU-domiciled individuals or companies for the multimodal models; 700M MAU clause retained. Allows synthetic-data generation and distillation.

Muse Spark, the first Meta Superintelligence Labs model (internally 'Avocado'), launched 2026-04-08 with no weights; Muse Spark 1.1 (2026-07-09) came with a public preview of a paid Meta Model API. Zuckerberg said Meta still intends to release open models alongside proprietary ones.

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Forced by the ASF's July 2017 ban on BSD+Patents code in Apache projects and developer backlash; React became the dominant front-end library under MIT.

relicensing_events.to: PyTorch Foundation under the Linux Foundation (same licence)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Governance, not licence, change. The foundation kept adding members (nine more announced Oct 2026).

relicensing_events.to: Llama 2 Community License (commercial use with 700M MAU cap)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Opened commercial use but stayed non-OSI; Fortune noted the 700M threshold walls off large rivals. Llama downloads reached 650M by Dec 2024, 1B by 2025-03-18 and 1.2B by late April 2025.

relicensing_events.to: React Foundation under the Linux Foundation (MIT)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Intent announced 2025-10-07 with Amazon, Callstack, Expo, Meta, Microsoft, Software Mansion and Vercel; formally launched 2026-02-24 with Huawei added.

relicensing_events.to: Closed-weight frontier model with paid API (Muse Spark)
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Reported from Dec 2025 (CNBC, Bloomberg) as a pivot driven by Meta Superintelligence Labs leadership and frustration that DeepSeek R1 drew on Llama's architecture; launched April 2026. Existing Llama weights remain available.

exit_events.note: Priced 2012-05-17 at $38/share, raising $16B; ~$104B valuation fully diluted (basic market cap figures ~$81-84B). First-day close $38.23.

risk_events: 2017-07: Apache Software Foundation classed React's BSD+Patents licence as Category X, forcing the Sept 2017 MIT relicense
2023-03-03: LLaMA weights leaked via 4chan within weeks of the gated research release; Meta answered with DMCA takedowns, then opened commercial use with Llama 2
2025: Llama 4's reception and DeepSeek R1's reuse of Llama architecture fed internal doubts about open weights; Meta Superintelligence Labs formed after the $14.3B Scale AI deal
2026-04-08: Pivot to closed frontier model (Muse Spark); developers who built on Llama face an uncertain open roadmap
2026: ~8,000-person layoff (May) and a $9.89B charge for an August 2026 multistate attorneys-general agreement (Q3 2026 results)
robustness: Very large, profitable single-vendor company (FY2025 revenue $201B). Its most widely used open projects no longer depend on Meta's strategy: PyTorch (Linux Foundation, since 2022) and React (React Foundation, since 2026) have multi-company boards, and OCP has had its own foundation since 2011. Llama, by contrast, is controlled solely by Meta, its licence is non-OSI, and the April 2026 closed Muse Spark launch shows the open-weights line can be deprioritised at will.
physical_science_relevance: PyTorch is the default deep-learning framework for scientific machine learning; Llama weights are widely fine-tuned for domain (including chemistry and materials) assistants because they can be run locally.
openness_effect_assessment: Openness made Meta's developer tools (React, PyTorch) industry standards, and Meta then handed them to neutral foundations, which locks in that adoption beyond Meta's control. Releasing Llama weights bought ecosystem reach (1B downloads by March 2025, 1.2B by April 2025) and a commoditize-the-complement position against closed API labs, but did not give Meta a frontier lead, and competitors (notably DeepSeek) built on its work. In 2026 Meta moved its frontier model behind a paid API, a sign that open weights were a tactic rather than a principle once it judged it could compete directly.
key_takeaway: Meta is the clearest example of commoditize-your-complement openness in AI: its money comes from advertising, so giving away frameworks and model weights cost little and undercut rivals whose business is selling model access. The record splits in two. Developer infrastructure was open-sourced and then put under neutral governance, which makes it robust. Model weights stayed under Meta's own non-OSI licence and were the first thing to close once the strategy changed. For the study, Meta shows that licence and governance, not the label 'open source', decide whether openness survives a change of corporate strategy.
